Monday, 2 October 2034. Amina and Bertrand Vidal meet the deputy mayor of Croix-Rousse to prepare the wedding ceremony, set for 14 October. Amina has, of course, brought a spreadsheet.
Have a seat. So you’re the couple the whole neighbourhood is talking about? The spreadsheet couple?
That’s us. Here is the document in which we’ve noted everything: the witnesses, the music and the silences.
The silences? That’s a request I wasn’t expecting. Explain.
After the “yes”, we would like eight bars of silence. It’s a tradition we’re very attached to.
Eight bars… And how will I know when they’re over?
Our conductor, Théo, will be at the back of the room. He’s the person you’ll be able to count on: he’ll beat time.
Very good. And the witnesses? They are the people with whom you will sign the register.
For me, it will be Julien Moreau, the director of the network thanks to which we met.
And for me, my brother Moussa. He’s coming from Dakar, a city to which our story is linked, in a way I’ll tell you about one day.
And the room? The wedding room is large, with a chandelier under which photos are often taken.
Perfect. For the party, we’ll go on to the Salle Hélène Morel. It’s the room where it all began.
(she smiles) You know, in twenty years I’ve never received a spreadsheet. I think this is the wedding I’ll remember the longest.

1. Lequel after a preposition
After a preposition (avec, pour, sur, dans, sans, par, sous), for THINGS you use “lequel”, which agrees with the noun:
Gender / number
l’archet avec lequel j’ai appris
la salle dans laquelle tout a commencé
les dossiers sur lesquels je travaille
les raisons pour lesquelles il est parti
In Romanian you simply say “care” or “în care”, “cu care”. In French you have to choose the form according to the gender and number of the preceding noun.
2. The contractions: auquel, duquel
With the prepositions “à” and “de”, lequel contracts (like le → au, du):
de + …
auquel (à + lequel)
duquel (de + lequel)
à laquelle (no contraction)
de laquelle (no contraction)
auxquels (à + lesquels)
desquels (de + lesquels)
auxquelles (à + lesquelles)
desquelles (de + lesquelles)
It’s a tradition we’re attached to. (tenir à)
The network thanks to which we met. (grâce à)
The concerts I attended. (assister à)
Verbs constructed with “à” require auquel / à laquelle: penser à, tenir à, s’attendre à, participer à, assister à, croire à.
3. People: “qui” after a preposition
For PEOPLE, after a preposition you usually use “qui” (simpler and more natural than lequel):
He’s the person you’ll be able to count on.
The friend I left with.
The colleague I spoke to.
The people with whom you’ll sign. (lequel is also possible for people, more formal)
After “parmi” and “entre” you MUST use lesquels, even for people: “les invités parmi lesquels il y avait le maire”.
4. “Dont” or “duquel”?
“Dont” replaces “de + noun” after a verb or a noun. But after a COMPOUND preposition (près de, à côté de, au milieu de, au-dessous de) you need “duquel / de laquelle”:
duquel / de laquelle
le couple dont tout le quartier parle (parler de)
l’école près de laquelle elle habite
le livre dont j’ai besoin (avoir besoin de)
le lustre au-dessous duquel on fait les photos
la ville dont il vient (venir de)
la place au milieu de laquelle se trouve l’arbre
“L’école près dont elle habite” ✗. After “près de”, “à côté de”, “au milieu de”, “à cause de” you cannot use “dont”!
5. “Où” for place and time
“Où” replaces an expression of place, but also of TIME, where Romanian uses “în care” or “când”:
It’s the room where it all began. (= dans laquelle)
On the day the letter arrived… (NOT “le jour quand”!)
The year I was born.
The town he comes from.
Typical mistake: “le jour quand” ✗ → “le jour où” ✓. After jour, moment, année, époque, instant you use “où”, not “quand”.

Huit mesures après le oui

Amina and Bertrand Vidal’s wedding had been set for Saturday 14 October 2034, at eleven o’clock, at the Croix-Rousse town hall. Amina had chosen the date for a reason she had explained to no one, and that no one had dared ask her about. Mr Vidal knew it. 14 October was the day, two years earlier, when the Court of Audit’s letter had arrived at the office. The day when everything had begun, without their knowing.

Of course there was a spreadsheet. There were in fact seven: the guests, the budget, the menu, the music, the seating plan, the schedule for the day and, since the end of the summer, the spreadsheet of silences, the one to which Mr Vidal had added his famous column. Amina worked on them in the evenings, in the little Croix-Rousse flat she had just moved into, and in which there were still only two chairs, a bed, a violin and a triangle.

The guest list had raised an unexpected problem. Amina, who had always said she had almost no family, had discovered while making the spreadsheet that she had far too much. Her mother, first of all, who had lived in Villeurbanne for forty years. Her three brothers, two of whom lived in Paris and one in Dakar. A dozen cousins, aunts, and a great-aunt of ninety-five who had announced she would come from Senegal, whatever the doctors said.

Amina’s mother was called Mariama Diallo. She was sixty-six. She had arrived in France at twenty-six, in 1994, with a husband, two children, a suitcase and a primary-teaching diploma that the authorities had refused to recognise. She had cleaned offices for fifteen years, in the Part-Dieu, in the evenings and at night. Then she had gone back to studying at forty-one and had become a primary teacher in Villeurbanne, at a school near which Mrs Roux lived.

Amina hardly ever talked about her mother. It wasn’t that they didn’t love each other. It was that they were too alike: two precise, silent women who counted everything and said nothing. When Amina had announced her engagement on the phone, her mother had simply replied: “It was about time.” Then she had asked how much he earned. Amina had given the exact figure. Her mother had said it was reasonable. It was her way of being happy.

On Mr Vidal’s side, the list was short. His parents were dead. He had a sister, Hélène, a maths teacher in Nancy, who would come with her husband and their two sons. There were also three colleagues from the regional audit chamber, with whom he had lunch every day, and Gérard Thiébaut, the luthier from Mirecourt, without whom, he had written in the spreadsheet, “none of this would have happened”. The old luthier was eighty-two. He had promised to come.

Hélène, Bertrand’s sister, had phoned the very evening he told her the news. She had cried for ten minutes, which wasn’t like her. Then she had said something Bertrand never forgot: “I thought you were going to die alone, between two files.” She was two years older than him. She remembered the day their father had sold the violin, in 1996. She had seen her little brother crying in his room all night, without making a sound.

Her two sons, thirteen-year-old twins, had asked to see the wedding spreadsheets. Amina had sent them, out of curiosity. The next day she received an email from the two boys, who had found three formula errors in the budget spreadsheet. Amina checked. They were right. She corrected the errors, then wrote to Hélène that her nephews were the only people, apart from their uncle, whom she would henceforth allow to touch her spreadsheets.

And then there were all the others. The fourteen Thursday ducks, who had insisted on playing during the ceremony. Julien, Ioana and the children. Isabelle. Théo and Lucia, Radu and little Yves. Inès and her mother. Claire Vasseur. Mrs Roux. Dr Lefèvre, with whom Amina had spent fifty-four evenings at the foot of the lime tree. Nathalie and Yves Le Goff, who would come from Brittany. In all, a hundred and twenty-three people. Amina had checked the figure four times.

Throughout September, the Thursday orchestra rehearsed the wedding silences. Théo took it very seriously. He had them play the waltz, then stopped everyone at the third verse, and timed it. Eight bars in three-four time, at the tempo of the waltz, came to exactly fourteen and a half seconds. Bernard Delorme found it hard to keep quiet for so long. It took six rehearsals before he managed it without blowing into his trumpet.

The next problem was the venue for the party. The town hall room was too small. The local restaurants were too expensive. It was Rose-Hélène who found the solution, one evening at dinner: why not the Salle Hélène Morel? That was where they had really met, where the triangle had sounded for the first time, where the spreadsheet of advantages and disadvantages had been read. Amina thought for three seconds. Then she opened a new spreadsheet.

On Saturday 7 October, a week before the wedding, Amina took Mr Vidal to her mother’s in Villeurbanne for the first time. She had put off this moment for four months, on various pretexts. She was afraid. Not that her mother wouldn’t like Bertrand: she was sure she would. She was afraid they would be too alike as well, and spend the afternoon in silence, looking at each other without a word, like two spreadsheets being compared.

That is exactly what happened. For the first hour, Mariama Diallo and Bertrand Vidal sat facing each other in the little living room with yellow curtains and drank mint tea in silence. Amina watched the clock. Her mother watched Bertrand. Bertrand watched the bookcase, in which there were hundreds of books, pupils’ exercise books and, on the top shelf, an old radio-cassette player from the seventies.

It was the radio-cassette player that changed everything. Bertrand asked whether it still worked. Mariama said yes, she had brought it back from Dakar in 1994, and it was the only object from her childhood she had kept. She took it down from the shelf. She put in a cassette. A Senegalese song from the seventies filled the living room, with guitars, percussion and a man’s voice singing in Wolof. Bertrand closed his eyes to listen.

When the song ended, he told, in his turn, the story of the Dakar cassette. The Marseille sailor, Henri, who played the harmonica on a ship in 1978 in the port of Dakar. The waltz, the eight-bar silence, the orchestras, the triangle. Mariama listened without moving. At one point she put down her cup. She asked, in a strange voice, whether Bertrand could play her the waltz. He had it on his phone, of course.

He played the original recording, the 1978 one, with Henri’s breathing, the wrong notes and Yves’s voice laughing in the background. Mariama listened to the first three notes. Then she leapt to her feet. Her hands were trembling. She said she knew this music. That she had heard it when she was ten, in the port of Dakar, where her father worked as a docker, one evening when a French ship was at the quay.

She remembered it perfectly, she said. She had come to bring her father his dinner in an iron mess tin. On the deck of the ship, a white sailor was playing the harmonica, sitting on a pile of ropes, and another, younger sailor was laughing and clapping his hands. The music was sad and joyful at the same time. At one point the sailor had stopped playing, for a long time, then started again. She had never forgotten that silence.

Amina had gone completely pale. She asked her mother why she had never told her this. Mariama replied that she had never thought about it again until today. It was one memory among thousands of others, tucked away in a corner of her mind, which she passed by without seeing. It had taken those three notes for it to resurface, intact, fifty-six years later, in a living room in Villeurbanne.

Bertrand called Yves Le Goff in Brittany that same evening. Yves listened to the story without a word. Then he said, in a hoarse voice, that he remembered that little girl very well. She was wearing a blue dress and carrying a mess tin bigger than herself. She had stopped on the quay to listen and hadn’t moved for the whole waltz. Henri had said, laughing, that at last he had an audience that didn’t talk during the silence. It was the only time in his life anyone had listened to him like that.

By the next day, the news had gone round everyone. Isabelle cried on the phone. Julien couldn’t believe it. Rose-Hélène found it perfectly normal. She said the waltz already knew everyone and was just waiting for people to notice. Amina, who believed only in figures, did the calculation: there was one chance in several million of such a coincidence happening. Then she closed the computer without adding anything.

Mariama, meanwhile, was sewing. She sewed at night, after marking her pupils’ work, in the little room where she had once raised her four children. Nobody was allowed in. She had bought the white fabric at the Croix-Rousse market and the gold thread in an African shop in the Guillotière. She embroidered the little triangles one by one, by hand, by the light of a desk lamp. There were three hundred and twelve of them. She had counted them.

On Thursday 12 October, two days before the wedding, the great-aunt arrived from Dakar. Her name was Fatou. She was ninety-five, almost blind, and had travelled alone, by plane, with a white cane and a gold-embroidered boubou folded in a cardboard suitcase. As she got off the plane she announced that she had married off eighteen nieces and great-nieces, and was not going to miss the last one, even if it meant crossing the sea.

At the airport, great-aunt Fatou came out last, on a flight attendant’s arm, with her white cane and her huge smile. Amina and Moussa were waiting for her. Fatou asked which of the two voices was the bride’s. Amina came closer. The old lady raised her hands and touched Amina’s face, for a long time, from forehead to chin, as if reading it. Then she said in Wolof: “You have your grandmother’s face. She counted everything too.”

On the Friday evening, Ioana had an idea. She video-called Grandma in Iași and handed her phone to great-aunt Fatou. The two old ladies didn’t speak a word of the same language. One was eighty-eight, the other ninety-five. One could hardly see any more, the other was hard of hearing. They talked for twenty minutes, each in her own language, laughing at the same moments. Nobody ever found out what about.

That night, Amina slept at her mother’s in Villeurbanne, in her old girlhood bedroom. She couldn’t sleep. Around midnight, her mother came in with two cups of tea and an old tin box. Inside were photos of Dakar from the seventies. The port, the ships, a little girl in a blue dress with a mess tin. Mariama hadn’t even known she had been photographed that day. Her father had taken the picture with a borrowed camera.

In the photo, behind the little girl, you could see the side of a white ship and, barely visible on deck, the blurred outline of a seated man, head bent, hands in front of his mouth. Amina looked at the photo for a very long time. Then she photographed it with her phone and sent it to Yves Le Goff in Brittany, at a quarter past midnight. Yves replied two minutes later. A single word: “Henri.”

Rose-Hélène, for her part, had been preparing her flowers since June. With Isabelle, she had gone every Sunday to the Parc de la Tête d’Or, under the old lime tree where Henri had picked his flower in 1962, to gather the fallen flowers. They had dried them in Odile’s flat on sheets of newspaper. By the end of the summer they had filled two baskets. Rose-Hélène had said it was so that Henri could be at the wedding a little too.

On Saturday 14 October, the weather was fine. A very blue, very cold autumn sky above the Croix-Rousse hill. By half past ten, the little square in front of the town hall was already full. The Thursday ducks had arrived first, with their instruments, and Bernard Delorme had put his 1975 band uniform back on, which was even a little tighter around the stomach. The baker had brought a triangle-shaped cake two metres long.

Mr Vidal arrived at a quarter to eleven, on foot, from his flat, as planned in the spreadsheet. He was wearing a suit. For the first time in his life, the suit was not grey. It was midnight blue, with a burgundy tie his sister Hélène had chosen for him. The Thursday ducks watched him arrive in stunned silence. Bernard Delorme said out loud that he wouldn’t have recognised him. Nobody contradicted him.

Amina arrived at two minutes to eleven, on the arm of her elder brother, Moussa, who had come from Dakar. She was wearing a dress her mother had sewn herself, all summer long, without telling her what it would look like: a long, very simple white dress with gold embroidery in the shape of little triangles on the collar and sleeves. When Amina had first seen it, the evening before, she had closed her bedroom door. For the fourth time in her life.

In the wedding room, Amina had drawn up a seating plan, of course. In the front row, the two families: Mariama, Fatou and Moussa on one side, Hélène, her husband and the twins on the other. Behind them, Julien, Ioana and the children, Isabelle, Gérard Thiébaut. Then the Thursday ducks, all of them, with their instruments in their cases. Mrs Roux was at the end of the front row in her wheelchair, with Lucien’s metronome on her knees.

The ceremony took place in the wedding room, a large room with wood-panelled walls, from whose ceiling hung a crystal chandelier. The deputy mayor, a smiling woman of about fifty, had received the spreadsheet of silences a week earlier. At first she had thought it was a joke. Then she had called Amina, who had explained to her, very seriously, that it wasn’t. The deputy mayor had promised to respect every bar.

She read the articles of the civil code. She asked Bertrand Vidal whether he took Amina Diallo as his wife. He answered yes, in a low, clear voice. She asked Amina the same question. Amina answered yes. And then, as planned in the spreadsheet, the deputy mayor fell silent. The whole room fell silent. Eight bars of silence, counted in three, at the exact tempo of Henri’s waltz, which Théo was discreetly beating with his hand at the back of the room.

In the middle of the silence, on the fifth bar, Amina took out of the sleeve of her dress a tiny silver triangle, no bigger than a thumb, which nobody had seen. She struck it once with a pin. Ting. The sound was tiny, barely audible. But in the silence of the wedding room, everyone heard it. And in the front row, Mariama Diallo put her hand to her mouth, like a little girl on a quay in Dakar.

At the end of the eighth bar, the deputy mayor spoke again. She declared them united in marriage. The witnesses signed: Julien for Bertrand, and Moussa for Amina. Then the couple signed, Amina with a pen she had brought, because she didn’t trust town-hall pens. And as they came out of the room onto the town-hall steps, under the blue sky, the Thursday ducks struck up Henri’s waltz.

Before they left, the deputy mayor asked the couple to stand under the crystal chandelier, beneath which every couple in Croix-Rousse had been photographed for a century. Amina looked at the chandelier suspiciously. She asked when it had last been checked. The deputy mayor burst out laughing. So did Bertrand. And it was that photo, with the couple laughing under a chandelier that might not be properly fixed, that Amina later had framed.

Rose-Hélène walked in front of them in a yellow dress, with a basket in which there were not rose petals, as at ordinary weddings, but dried lime flowers. It was her idea. She threw them into the air by the handful above the newlyweds, and the autumn wind carried them along the street. Henri-Ion followed her with a second, smaller basket, whose contents he was discreetly eating. Little Yves, aged two, was asleep in his pushchair.

The party began at one o’clock in the Salle Hélène Morel, which the Thursday ducks had decorated all week. Strings of lights hung under the big skylight. On each table there was a little pot with a young lime tree, which each guest would take home on leaving, to plant. It was Dr Lefèvre’s idea. Amina had agreed after checking that the Drôme nursery could supply a hundred and twenty-three.

The meal had been prepared by three different cooks, which had required a separate spreadsheet. Mariama and her sisters had made thieboudienne, the Senegalese national dish, with fish, red rice and vegetables, in pots so big that they had to be transported in Bernard Delorme’s van. The baker had made the triangle cake. And Yves Le Goff, aged ninety, had made the galettes, with Nathalie as his assistant, to applause.

Moussa gave the first speech. He spoke in French, then in Wolof, so that the great-aunt would understand. He told how his little sister, at six, arranged her toys by size and kept a notebook of the sweets she was given. He said the whole family had wondered for thirty years what man could put up with a woman who counted sweets. Then he raised his glass to Bertrand. He said: “A man who counts silences.”

Hélène spoke next. She told the story of the violin sold in 1996, and the night her little brother had cried without a sound. She said she had waited thirty-eight years to hear him play again. Then she turned to Gérard Thiébaut, at the back of the room, and to Amina, beside her brother. She thanked them both, in a trembling voice, for giving her brother back to her. The whole Thursday-ducks table was crying. Even Bernard Delorme.

It was during the meal that Gérard Thiébaut gave his present. He stood up, leaning on his cane, and went over to the newlyweds’ table with a long, narrow case of varnished wood. He put it down in front of Bertrand. Inside was a bow. An old, very slender bow of pernambuco wood, with an ebony and silver frog. The luthier explained that it was the bow with which he himself had learnt the violin, in 1960, and that he had kept it ever since for an occasion he had never believed would come.

Bertrand refused, of course. A magistrate could not accept a gift of such value. Gérard Thiébaut smiled. He said he wasn’t giving it to the magistrate. He was giving it to the violinist. And that anyway the violinist had no choice, since it was no longer a gift but an inheritance. He added that he was eighty-two, and that you don’t argue with an old man on a wedding day. Bertrand said nothing more.

Around four o’clock, Théo signalled to the Thursday ducks. They set up under the skylight with their instruments. Bertrand took his Mirecourt violin and the new bow. Amina took her triangle, the big one from the concert. And Théo announced that the orchestra would play Henri’s waltz. But not as usual. This time, he said, there would be two silences: Henri’s, at the third verse, and another at the end, which the couple had requested.

They played. Bertrand played with Gérard’s bow, and everyone noticed that the sound of his violin had changed: rounder, warmer, as if the bow remembered something. At the third verse, the orchestra stopped. Eight bars. Amina struck her triangle on the fifth. And when Rose-Hélène raised her harmonica to play the three notes, someone in the front row began to sing.

It was Mariama. She sang in Wolof, in a low, deep voice that nobody in the room, not even Amina, had ever heard from her. She sang the three notes of the waltz, but with words, words she made up as she went along, which great-aunt Fatou, sitting beside her, repeated after her, clapping softly. Rose-Hélène lowered her harmonica. She understood at once that this lady must be allowed to sing.

Later, Moussa translated the words for those who didn’t speak Wolof. Mariama had sung: “I was little on the quay; the sailor played for the sea. He fell silent, and I waited. Fifty-six years I waited for the rest. Today my daughter has found it.” Then Mariama had fallen silent in her turn. And only then had Rose-Hélène whistled the next three notes, and the orchestra started again.

The second silence, the one at the end, also lasted exactly eight bars. During that silence, Bertrand put down his violin. Amina put down her triangle. They looked at each other. And in front of a hundred and twenty-three people, for the first time in public, they held hands. Just that. No kiss, no speech. Two hands, one in the other, in the middle of an eight-bar silence. The whole room understood that it was the most important moment of the day.

The party went on until midnight. People danced to Senegalese music, to waltzes, to brass-band tunes, to a Romanian song that Sorina played on the piano while Andrei, who had come from London, watched her with eyes everyone noticed. Bernard Delorme opened the champagne he had lost in the bet. Mrs Roux danced in her wheelchair, pushed by Inès. And great-aunt Fatou recounted, to anyone who would listen, her eighteen previous weddings.

Bertrand danced very badly. He knew it, and had even noted it in the spreadsheet, in the risks column. Amina couldn’t dance at all. So they did what they knew how to do: they counted. One, two, three, one, two, three, under their breath, looking at their feet. The whole room stopped to watch them. After three minutes they were no longer counting. They were dancing. Badly, but together.

Then Isabelle played a little piece on the cello, alone, under the skylight. She had been learning the cello for eighteen months. It wasn’t perfect. But she played to the end without stopping, eyes closed, and when she had finished, Gérard Thiébaut was the first to stand up and applaud. He said out loud that Henri had been right: she had a cellist’s hands. Like her mother. Isabelle couldn’t answer.

Around nine o’clock, the children had fallen asleep under the tables, on the guests’ coats. Henri-Ion, little Yves and Amina’s two youngest cousins formed a heap of arms and legs at the foot of the newlyweds’ table. Rose-Hélène refused to sleep. She had decided she would stay awake until the last silence. She managed it. She fell asleep four minutes later, on the knees of Mariama, whom she had only known since the morning.

Around ten o’clock, Yves Le Goff asked to speak to Mariama alone. They sat in a corner of the room, the old Breton sailor and the Senegalese teacher, and talked for a long time about Dakar, the port, the ships, the year 1978. Yves told her that Henri had remembered the little girl with the mess tin all his life. He called her “our best audience”. Mariama cried. So did Yves. Then they both laughed, like two children.

Before leaving, Mariama did something Amina would never forget. She took her daughter aside, by the big skylight, under the October stars. She told her she was proud of her. That all her life she had been afraid she hadn’t told her enough. That she counted too much and spoke too little, like her. And that today, hearing the little silver triangle, she had understood that Amina had found a way of saying things without speaking.

At the end of the evening, Bertrand announced in front of everyone where they would go on honeymoon in December. It was neither Venice nor Paris. It was Dakar. Amina wanted to see the port where her mother had heard the waltz. Bertrand wanted to see the quay where Henri had played. And Mariama had decided to go with them, to show them the exact spot. Moussa said it was the first honeymoon in history with a mother-in-law as guide. Everyone laughed.

The last guest left at a quarter past midnight. It was Gérard Thiébaut, who had missed his train and whom Bernard Delorme was going to drive back to Mirecourt in his van, in the middle of the night, because he had said he didn’t mind. In the empty hall, all that remained were the newlyweds, the strings of lights, the cleared tables and a single little potted lime tree, forgotten on a chair. Amina picked it up. She said they would plant it at their home.

Walking back towards Croix-Rousse in the cold night, Bertrand carried the violin and the bow, Amina carried the triangle and the little lime tree. They didn’t talk. They didn’t need to. When they reached their building, Amina stopped under a street lamp. She took out her phone. Bertrand thought she was going to check one last spreadsheet. He looked at the screen over her shoulder. She had opened a new file. It was empty. It was simply called: “Us”.

He asked her what she was going to put in it. Amina thought for a long time, under the street lamp, the little lime tree in her arms. Then she replied that she didn’t know. That it was the first time in her life she had opened a spreadsheet without knowing what columns it would have. Bertrand smiled. He said it was probably the only spreadsheet that would never need checking. Amina nodded. Then she closed the file without writing anything. And they went upstairs.

The speech Julien gave at Amina and Bertrand’s wedding as the groom’s witness. Notice the compound relative pronouns. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Le discours du témoin
Dear friends, two years ago a letter arrived at the office. It was a letter from the Court of Audit, because of which I didn’t sleep for a week. Amina, on the other hand, smiled.

A few days later, a grey man walked into the small room, at the back of which Amina had prepared two hundred and fourteen spreadsheets. He was the inspector with whom she would work for three weeks, almost without speaking.
I didn’t know those silences were the beginning of a conversation in which nobody else took part. A conversation in which people spoke in figures, in black coffees, in added sugars.
Then there was a violin, thanks to which Bertrand found a part of himself he had lost at fourteen. And a triangle, with which Amina learnt that sometimes a single note is enough.
Today we are gathered in the room where their story really began, under the window through which the light comes in. It is a room in the middle of which there has always been a silence.
I raise my glass to the two most precise people I know, to whom I owe the understanding that love, too, can be counted in bars. To Amina and Bertrand!
